clinicalPearls: Characterised by recurrent crops of intensely pruritic vesiculopustules on the palms, soles and lateral aspects of the hands and feet in infants and toddlers.
Lesions appear in episodic waves lasting one to two weeks, then clear, with symptom-free intervals of several weeks before the next crop.
The intense itch is disproportionate to the modest number of lesions and often causes marked irritability and disturbed sleep.
A strong association exists with preceding scabies, and the condition is thought in many cases to be a persistent hypersensitivity reaction after treated infestation.
Cytology of a pustule shows a predominance of neutrophils, sometimes with eosinophils, and no organisms, helping to distinguish it from infection.
The disorder is self-limiting and tends to resolve by two to three years of age with progressively less frequent and milder episodes.
Potent topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines reduce itch and inflammation during flares; dapsone is reserved for severe refractory disease.
Persistent acral pustules should always prompt reassessment for active scabies in the child and close contacts before attributing them to acropustulosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile acropustulosis is a benign, recurrent, sterile pustular dermatosis of unknown precise cause. It is characterised histologically by intraepidermal or subcorneal pustules filled with neutrophils, often admixed with eosinophils, without evidence of infection. A widely accepted view is that in a substantial proportion of cases the disorder represents a prolonged id-type or hypersensitivity response of the infant skin following scabies infestation, even after the mites have been successfully eradicated, with the acral skin showing an exaggerated inflammatory reactivity. The episodic, self-limiting nature and eventual spontaneous resolution suggest maturation of immune regulation with age. There is no systemic involvement and the pustules are consistently sterile on culture.
additionalInvestigations: skin scrapings and dermoscopy to exclude active scabies
pustule smear cytology (Tzanck-type preparation) showing neutrophils with or without eosinophils
Gram stain and bacterial culture of pustule contents to exclude infection
potassium hydroxide microscopy to exclude dermatophyte or candidal pustules
full blood count with differential where peripheral eosinophilia is queried
skin biopsy in atypical or persistent cases
examination and treatment history review of household contacts for scabies
redFlags: burrows, family itch or persistent lesions indicating untreated active scabies
fever, spreading erythema or crusting suggesting secondary bacterial infection
failure to enter remission between crops, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
widespread or systemic pustulation raising concern for other pustular disorders
significant sleep disruption and distress requiring escalation of symptom control
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; the condition is entirely benign and self-limiting, with flares becoming less frequent and less severe over time and complete resolution usually by around two to three years of age.
pitfalls: failing to look for and treat active scabies in the child and contacts
misinterpreting sterile pustules as bacterial infection and giving repeated unnecessary antibiotics
under-treating the severe pruritus, leading to excoriation and secondary infection
confusing recurrent crops with an evolving neonatal pustular condition rather than a distinct entity
reaching for dapsone before optimising topical corticosteroids and antihistamines
management: Symptomatic control of flares with potent topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and itch
Oral antihistamines to relieve the intense pruritus and improve sleep
Exclusion and treatment of active scabies with a topical scabicide such as permethrin, as infestation frequently precedes the condition
Avoidance of repeated unnecessary antiscabetic treatment once active infestation has been excluded
Consideration of dapsone for severe or refractory disease
Reassurance that the disorder is benign and self-limiting, with resolution usually by early childhood, and clinical follow-up of recurrent crops
